title: A Script for the Test Day: Timed Events From a Text File, and Delivering Each Exactly Once

questions.question: Why describe a test as text and not as code?
options: Text is parsed faster than C++ is compiled, so the tests run sooner
A text file cannot contain a mistake that stops the run, where code can
Text is checked into the repository, and code is not
A person who has never built the repository can read and change it, the same file runs against simulation and bench, and a bug from the robot is reproduced by adding lines
questions.explanation: A scenario written as lines of text can be written by whoever saw the fault, and the same file drives the simulation and the bench.

questions.question: A script has a mistake on lines 2, 3, 4 and 5. What should the parser do?
options: Stop at line 2 and report it, so that the first mistake is fixed first
Skip the bad lines and run the scenario with the good ones
Report all of them with their line numbers and leave the scenario empty: a half read script that runs is worse than none
Report the last one, since later lines depend on earlier ones
questions.explanation: Stopping at the first makes a person fix them one run at a time. And a scenario built from the good lines only is a different test from the one written.

questions.question: A time is written 1.5e. What should the parser do?
options: Read it as 1.5 and carry on, as std::stod does
Refuse it: a number is the whole word or it is an error, since reading 1.5 would run a scenario different from the one written
Read it as 15, treating the e as an exponent of 1
Read it as zero, the default for a bad number
questions.explanation: A word that is not wholly a number is an error. Taking the part that parses changes the scenario without telling anyone.

questions.question: Which events does the step from t0 to t1 take?
options: Those from t0 to t1 including both ends, so that none is missed
Those after t0 and up to and including t1: so consecutive steps cover the line with no gap and no overlap
Those strictly between t0 and t1, so that none is taken twice
Those at or after t0 and before t1
questions.explanation: Half open intervals tile the time line. Including both ends would deliver an event on a boundary twice; excluding both would never deliver it.

questions.question: The first target is at time 0. Why might a simulation never apply it?
options: An event at zero is treated as a comment
The parser refuses a time of zero
The first step is skipped while the simulation starts up
The first interval starts at 0, and an interval that excludes its start has no place for an event at 0: events_between(0, 0.01) gave nothing and events_between(-1, 0.01) gave it
questions.explanation: With the rule t0 < time <= t1, the interval from 0 to 0.01 does not contain 0. Starting the first interval before zero gives the event a home.

questions.question: An event at 1.0 s and steps of 0.1 s arrives at step 11 in one run and 10 in another. What differs?
options: How the step's time was worked out: adding 0.1 ten times gives 0.9999999999999999, short of 1.0, and the step number times 0.1 gives 1.0
The parser read the event's time as 1.1 in one run
The scenario was sorted differently in the two runs
One run used a step of 0.09 by mistake
questions.explanation: 0.1 has no exact binary form, and ten of them added fall just short of 1.0. The step number times the step lands on it.
